channel_name: The Compound and Friends · Josh Brown
video_title: Why Every Trader on Earth is Watching the 10-Year Treasury Now | WDWL
gist: Nick Colas of DataTrek walks Josh Brown's audience through why long Treasury yields broke out: it is entirely real rates, not inflation expectations, driven by the QE unwind, a higher neutral rate implied by five years without a recession, deficits, and AI-related corporate bond supply crowding out Treasury demand. He tells clients to stay under five years of duration until the economy weakens, flags 5% on the 10-year as the level where equities jitter, and lays out three 12-month scenarios for the index (+6-16% base, +13-28% on a US-Iran resolution and lower oil, +12-39% if AI capex shows up in earnings). Underneath it he argues the whole AI capex cycle is a bet on reaching AGI first, and that public equity investing has become VC-like with tech at 38% of MSCI ACWI.

themes.theme: Long-end yields are a real-rate story

insights.claim: The 30-year Treasury's breakout to 15-20 year high yields is entirely a real-rate move, not an inflation scare: decomposed breakeven inflation expectations have been dead flat between roughly 1.5% and 2.5% since 2010 while real yields pushed from ~2-2.5% up toward 3%.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: Kills the 'inflation is back' narrative for the long end and points positioning toward real-rate hedges rather than inflation hedges.
insights.quote: the red line which is inflation expectations has been dead flat pretty much for the last 15 16 years

insights.claim: Colas attributes climbing long-end real rates to four forces: the unwind of Fed QE that had artificially depressed them, a higher neutral rate implied by the absence of recession, persistently high federal deficits, and AI-related long-term corporate borrowing pulling demand away from Treasuries.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: Three of the four drivers are structural rather than cyclical, arguing the long end stays elevated even if the Fed cuts the front end.
insights.quote: there's a lot of air related long-term corporate borrowing going on and that's pulling demand away from treasuries

insights.claim: TLT compounded at almost +8% a year with coupons reinvested through the 2010s but has a negative 4.4% compound annual growth rate so far in the 2020s, turning the standard long-duration portfolio hedge into a persistent drag.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: A hard number for advisors defending a strategic long-Treasury sleeve; the risk-off anchor has been destroying returns for six years.
insights.quote: your kager, your compound annual growth rate over this decade so far has been negative 4.4%

insights.claim: Colas is telling DataTrek clients to keep portfolio duration short — under five years — until the US economy actually weakens, describing the fixed income structure as a step stool rather than a ladder out to 30 years.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: An explicit, actionable duration call from an institutional research shop: stay short until labor and growth data crack.
insights.quote: you got to keep on portfolio durations pretty short, like under five years until the US economy weakens

insights.claim: The absence of any US recession since 2020 despite aggressive 2022 rate hikes, a 2025 trade policy shock and two oil shocks forces the conclusion that the neutral rate of interest is structurally higher than history suggests.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: If r-star is genuinely higher, the terminal fed funds rate and fair-value long yields both reset upward — a repricing that cuts across every asset class.
insights.quote: the neutral rate of interest, the rate at which the Fed keeps rates over a cycle, must be higher than historically has been the case

themes.theme: AI bond supply crowding out Treasuries

insights.claim: US corporate bond issuance is running about $1.75 trillion this year, roughly 20-30% ahead of the same point in 2025, driven by hyperscalers financing AI buildouts.
insights.speaker: host (The Compound, 'What Did We Learn?')
insights.so_what: Sizes the new competing supply of high-grade duration — the mechanical source of upward pressure on Treasury yields.
insights.quote: I think the number is 1.75 trillion in corporate bond issuance this year

insights.claim: Colas argues every dollar into a high-grade corporate bond is a dollar not into a Treasury, and that a bond investor can reasonably view Google's cash flows as at least as safe as the US government's taxing power.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: If mega-cap credit is treated as a Treasury substitute, the risk-free benchmark itself faces competition — structurally higher Treasury yields and tighter mega-cap spreads.
insights.quote: Google I think I I could argue is at least as safe as the US government because it's a global business and very well-managed

insights.claim: The mega caps have flipped from buyback-and-dividend companies to secondary stock and debt issuers, and the host notes it is no accident that Oracle is the worst-performing mega cap and the only one with a debt rating nearly cut to junk.
insights.speaker: host (The Compound, 'What Did We Learn?')
insights.so_what: Identifies leverage as the differentiator within big tech — screen mega caps by roll risk and issuance rather than treating them as one bloc.
insights.quote: I don't think it's an accident that Oracle is the worst performing mega cap stock and is also the loan mega cap stock with a debt rating that's almost been cut to junk

insights.claim: The hyperscalers' underlying cash flows funding all this AI debt are still cyclical — advertising and high-end electronics — exactly the revenue that contracts in a recession.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: The credit case for AI debt rests on cyclical revenue, so a consumer or ad slowdown transmits straight into AI-linked credit spreads.
insights.quote: the current cash flows of the hyperscalers are still economically sensitive. It's advertising. It's high-end electronics

insights.claim: Colas watches 5% on the 10-year Treasury as the level where borrowing costs begin to threaten growth and earnings and equities start to jitter; the 10-year is at roughly 4.70-4.72% today, so the trigger is close but not hit.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: A specific, monitorable level for de-risking equities — roughly 30 basis points of headroom from current yields.
insights.quote: If you get to 5% on tens, there's the threat the economy slows down because borrowing costs are higher

insights.claim: Against the argument that the 1990s averaged a 5% ten-year yield alongside a booming economy, Colas counters that the 1990s were a descent from ~15-17% peaks under Volcker, a massive tailwind, whereas today's move is 0% to 5% with no natural cap on the upside.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: Direction of travel, not the static level, determines whether a 5% yield is benign — an argument against 1990s analogies used to dismiss current rate risk.
insights.quote: This is not that. This is coming from 0 to 5. And where does it stop? We don't know yet

insights.claim: Colas says that if investors could be guaranteed the 10-year stops at 5% for the rest of the decade, equity multiples would expand by two points tomorrow — the uncertainty about the terminal yield, not the yield itself, is what caps valuations.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: Frames rate uncertainty as a quantifiable multiple discount — roughly 2 turns of P/E available on any credible cap to long yields.
insights.quote: if we could guarantee a listener, hey, that the 10's going to stop at five for the rest of the decade. Multiples would expand by two points tomorrow

insights.claim: Higher rates and multiple expansion can coexist because valuation is C over R minus G: if earnings growth accelerates from low teens to high teens, that more than offsets a rise in the discount rate from 5% to 6%.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: A rebuttal to the reflexive 'rates up, multiples down' trade — growth acceleration is the variable that lets equities absorb higher yields.
insights.quote: the higher the growth rate is, the valuation can be higher. It's C over R minus G for the nerds in the audience

insights.claim: DataTrek's valuation grid applies a 14x-22x ten-year multiple range plus a 24x dot-com peak and a 26x dream case to consensus earnings, and most of the grid produces losses from current levels — real payoffs only appear at 20x-plus.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: Shows the index is priced for the upper half of its own historical multiple range, leaving little cushion for an earnings miss or a confidence wobble.
insights.quote: You only get to real payoffs at 20 plus times earnings

insights.claim: The index is up about 12.1% year to date entirely on earnings revisions — up 15% for this year and 13% for next — with slight P/E contraction rather than any multiple expansion.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: The rally is fundamentally supported rather than sentiment-driven, which makes the earnings revision trend the single most important thing to monitor.
insights.quote: It has been no PE expansion at all. As a matter of fact, you had a little PE contraction

insights.claim: Colas, a sell-side analyst in the 1990s who has watched the data for 30 years, says analysts essentially never raise numbers during a year — they start high and trim — making this year's upward revisions historically unusual.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: Breaking a 30-year behavioral pattern is a genuine signal of underlying strength — and its reversal would be an early warning.
insights.quote: Analysts never raise numbers during a year. It just never happens. They start high and trim

insights.claim: Colas's base case is +6% to +16% over the next 12 months, requiring only that earnings estimates keep rising and the multiple stays flat around 20x.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: A concrete central forecast with no multiple expansion assumed — a benchmark against which to judge more bullish sell-side targets.
insights.quote: Multiples stay flat at around 20. And you get six to 16% upside

insights.claim: The bull-ish middle case of +13% to +28% requires a resolution to the US-Iran conflict, lower oil and diesel prices and a 22x multiple; Colas says this was his base case until about six weeks ago and the ongoing conflict has pushed him down to the 6-16% band.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: Makes oil and Middle East de-escalation the explicit swing factor between a mid-single-digit and a high-teens equity year.
insights.quote: Honestly, this was my base case until about six weeks ago

insights.claim: The maximum bull case of +12% to +39% at a 24x multiple requires earnings growth, lower oil, and AI capex finally showing up as visible value in tech earnings — all three simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: Defines what a melt-up actually requires, so investors can score the probability rather than assume it.
insights.quote: you can get to a 24 multiple and then you're talking 12 to 39% upside

insights.claim: Colas says AI has exploded this year for one reason — coding — and that the non-coding majority of the economy has to start working for the investment case to hold.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: Narrows the demonstrated AI TAM to a single workflow, making enterprise non-coding adoption the key datapoint for whether current capex is justified.
insights.quote: AI has exploded this year for one reason. It's coding

themes.theme: The AGI race is the actual thesis

insights.claim: Colas argues that what equity investors are buying in AI is 100% the race to artificial general intelligence, not agents or coding assistants, and that this is why the capex is being spent.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: Reframes AI capex as a winner-take-most option on AGI rather than an ROI-per-project question — which is why near-term ROI critiques keep failing to move the stocks.
insights.quote: What you're investing in right now is 100% about getting to AGI as soon as possible. That's the game

insights.claim: Citing artificialanalysis.ai, Colas notes ChatGPT's measured intelligence is up 1300% since its November 2022 launch and Claude improved 76% in the last year, far exceeding Moore's Law's ~41% annual pace.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: A quantified capability curve that underwrites the capex case — a visible deceleration in these benchmarks would be the thesis-breaking datapoint.
insights.quote: Since November 22 when it launched, Chat GPT's intelligence is up 1300%. In the last year, clause has improved by 76%

insights.claim: Colas's reserve-currency framework holds that the dollar's status derives from what US society does with its capital — innovation — rather than from the military and taxation, so a deficit is sustainable only while innovation expands the tax base.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: Links the AI race directly to the dollar and Treasury demand: losing AI leadership becomes a fiscal and currency problem, not just a tech-sector one.
insights.quote: the reason the US dollar is a reserve currency is because of the innovation in the US

insights.claim: Sixteen of the world's twenty most valuable companies by market cap are American, and the other four sit in Asia and the Netherlands as effective offshoots of US tech.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: Quantifies how concentrated global equity value is in the US innovation complex — and therefore how much rides on the AI race outcome.
insights.quote: 16 of the top most valuable global companies by market cap are US companies

insights.claim: Colas argues that even if Chinese champions win the AI race, investors will not capture the returns because Beijing constrains how much its companies can earn — only the western system allows the winners to monetize fully.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: A reason to underweight Chinese AI equities even on a bullish technology view: the technology can win while the equity does not.
insights.quote: you won't even be able to make a lot of money if BYU wins or Baba wins or 10-centent wins or deepseek wins

themes.theme: Market structure: low correlations, VC-like equities

insights.claim: S&P sector and stock correlations are at ten-plus year lows, which Colas attributes to a widespread belief in a recession-proof US economy that lets investors pick sectors freely and keeps aggregate volatility and the VIX suppressed.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: Low correlation is a bet on no recession — the setup where a growth scare causes correlations and volatility to spike violently together.
insights.quote: correlations are extremely low like crazy low. We measure them sector- wise they're at 10 plus year lows

insights.claim: Colas says the hyperscalers implicitly assume no recession for the next five years — otherwise they would not be leveraging their balance sheets to spend — and that being long this market requires believing that assumption completely.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: States the single embedded assumption underneath both the capex cycle and the equity market, giving investors one variable to stress-test.
insights.quote: assumption of this market and the investment cycle that we're in is that there is no recession for the next 5 years. Period. Full stop

insights.claim: Public equity investing has become VC-like: the top of the index used to return a third to a half of cash flows via buybacks and dividends, and now every dollar goes into a science project, with tech at 38% of MSCI ACWI.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: Investors holding a global index are now running a levered venture bet whether they intended to or not — the shareholder-yield component has largely disappeared.
insights.quote: We're back to a VC kind of investment cycle where every single dollar these companies make is going to a science project

insights.claim: Colas, a long-standing skeptic of equal-weight S&P exposure, now sees a point to it because equal weight is 14% tech versus 38% for cap-weighted global indices, keeping the exposure without the leverage.
insights.speaker: Nick Colas, DataTrek Research co-founder
insights.so_what: A named skeptic changing his mind on equal-weight is a tradeable signal for anyone looking to dial down AI concentration risk without exiting tech.
